items.stem: An alternating current is given by I = 5.0 sin(314t) A. What is its frequency?
items.answer: 50 Hz
items.markingKey: ω = 314 rad s⁻¹ = 2πf.

items.stem: Explain why a sinusoidal alternating current transfers energy to a resistor even though its mean value over a cycle is zero.
items.answer: The power I²R depends on the square of the current, which is always positive; energy is transferred in both halves of the cycle regardless of current direction.
items.markingKey: P = I²R, always positive [1]; energy in both half-cycles [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how an oscilloscope is used to measure the peak voltage and frequency of an alternating supply.
items.answer: Connect the supply to the Y-input; measure the height from centre to peak in divisions × Y-gain (V div⁻¹) for V₀; measure the horizontal length of one cycle × time-base (s div⁻¹) for T, then f = 1/T.
items.markingKey: peak from divisions × Y-gain [1]; period from divisions × time-base, f = 1/T [1] [2]

items.stem: An oscilloscope displays a sinusoidal trace. The time-base is 0.50 ms div⁻¹ and the Y-gain is 0.50 V div⁻¹. One complete cycle occupies 2.0 divisions horizontally, and the trace extends 1.5 divisions above and below the centre line. Determine the frequency of the signal.
items.markingKey: T = 2.0 × 0.50 ms = 1.0 ms; f = 1/T = 1000 Hz. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An oscilloscope displays a sinusoidal trace. The time-base is 1.0 ms div⁻¹ and the Y-gain is 5.0 V div⁻¹. One complete cycle occupies 2.5 divisions horizontally, and the trace extends 2.0 divisions above and below the centre line. Determine the period, the frequency and the peak voltage.
items.answer: T = 2.5 ms; f = 400 Hz; V₀ = 10 V
items.markingKey: T = divisions × time-base = 2.5 ms [1]; f = 1/T = 400 Hz [1]; V₀ = 2.0 × 5.0 = 10 V [1] [3]

items.stem: A sinusoidal alternating supply has a peak p.d. of 17 V and a frequency of 60 Hz. It is displayed on an oscilloscope. (a) Calculate the angular frequency. (b) Suggest suitable time-base and Y-gain settings to display two complete cycles filling about 10 horizontal and 6 vertical divisions. (c) State the peak-to-peak p.d.
items.answer: (a) 377 rad s⁻¹ (b) time-base about 3.3 ms div⁻¹; Y-gain about 5.7 V div⁻¹ (c) 34 V
items.markingKey: (a) ω = 2πf: 377 rad s⁻¹ [1] (b) time-base [1]; Y-gain [1] [2] (c) 2V₀: 34 V [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the root-mean-square value of an alternating current?
options: the maximum value of the current
the steady direct current that dissipates the same mean power in a resistor
the average value of the current over one cycle
items.answer: the steady direct current that dissipates the same mean power in a resistor
items.markingKey: I_rms gives the same heating effect as an equal d.c.

items.stem: Show that the mean power in a resistor carrying a sinusoidal current is half the peak power.
items.answer: P = I²R = I₀²R sin²ωt; the mean value of sin²ωt over a cycle is ½, so mean P = ½I₀²R = ½P₀.
items.markingKey: P ∝ sin² [1]; mean of sin² = ½ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the r.m.s. value is used rather than the mean value to describe an alternating current.
items.answer: The mean value of a sinusoidal current over a cycle is zero, which says nothing about its heating effect; the r.m.s. value is the equivalent steady current giving the same mean power.
items.markingKey: mean value is zero [1]; r.m.s. equivalent d.c. for heating [1] [2]

items.stem: A sinusoidal supply of r.m.s. voltage 110 V is connected across a 100 Ω resistor. Calculate the peak voltage.
items.markingKey: V₀ = √2 × V_rms = √2 × 110 = 156 V. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Explain why a lamp connected to a 50 Hz supply does not appear to flicker even though its power varies.
items.answer: The power varies at 100 Hz (twice per cycle) and the filament stays hot between peaks; the eye cannot detect such rapid changes.

items.stem: What is meant by rectification?
options: the conversion of alternating current into direct current
the conversion of direct current into alternating current
increasing the voltage of a supply
the smoothing of a varying d.c. output
items.answer: the conversion of alternating current into direct current
items.markingKey: Rectifiers allow current in one direction only.

items.stem: Explain how a single capacitor smooths the output of a rectifier.
items.answer: When the rectified p.d. rises the capacitor charges to the peak; as the p.d. falls the diode stops conducting and the capacitor discharges through the load, keeping the p.d. near the peak until the next pulse recharges it.
items.markingKey: charges at peak [1]; discharges slowly through load between peaks [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why full-wave rectification gives a smoother output than half-wave rectification for the same smoothing capacitor and load.
items.answer: The capacitor is recharged twice as often (every half-cycle), so it discharges for a shorter time between peaks and the ripple is smaller.
items.markingKey: twice as many pulses [1]; less time to discharge, smaller ripple [1] [2]

items.stem: The output of a full-wave rectifier connected to a 60 Hz supply has a peak value of 17 V. A 220 μF smoothing capacitor is connected across a 10 kΩ load. Calculate the time constant of the load and capacitor.
items.markingKey: τ = RC = 10 000 × 2.20 × 10⁻⁴ = 2.2 s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The output of a full-wave rectifier connected to a 60 Hz supply has a peak value of 17 V. A 220 μF smoothing capacitor is connected across a 4.7 kΩ load. Calculate the time between successive peaks of the output and the time constant, and comment on whether the smoothing is effective.
items.answer: 8.33 ms; τ = 1.03 s; τ ≫ time between peaks, so smoothing is good
items.markingKey: interval = 8.33 ms [1]; τ = RC = 1.03 s [1]; τ ≫ interval, small ripple [1] [3]

items.stem: A bridge rectifier is connected to a 50 Hz supply of peak voltage 10 V (ignore p.d.s across the diodes). The output is connected to a 2.0 kΩ load with a 220 μF capacitor in parallel. (a) State the purpose of the four diodes. (b) Describe the output without the capacitor. (c) Explain why the time constant must be much larger than 10 ms for good smoothing.
items.answer: (a) Full-wave rectification: current through the load in one direction in both half-cycles. (b) Half-sine pulses, all positive, 100 per second, peak 10 V. (c) Then the capacitor loses only a small fraction of its charge between peaks.
items.markingKey: (a) Full-wave rectification: current through the load in one direction in both half-cycles [1] (b) all positive pulses [1]; 100 Hz [1] [2] (c) Then the capacitor loses only a small fraction of its charge between peaks [1]

items.stem: How many diodes are used in a bridge rectifier?
items.answer: four
items.markingKey: A full-wave bridge uses four diodes.

items.stem: Describe how the four diodes in a bridge rectifier ensure the current through the load is always in the same direction.
items.answer: In each half-cycle a different pair of opposite diodes conducts, both routing the current through the load in the same direction; the other pair is reverse-biased.
items.markingKey: two diodes conduct each half-cycle [1]; same direction through load both halves [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain the effect on the ripple of increasing the load resistance with the same smoothing capacitor.
items.answer: The time constant RC increases, so the capacitor discharges more slowly between peaks and the ripple voltage decreases.
items.markingKey: RC larger [1]; slower discharge, smaller ripple [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe and explain the effect on the output p.d. across the load when the single diode in a half-wave rectifier is reversed.
items.answer: The other half of each cycle passes: the output pulses are negative instead of positive (same shape and frequency).
items.markingKey: correct description of output [1]; explanation [1]; quantitative comment (frequency or ripple size) [1] [3]

items.stem: Describe and explain the effect on the output p.d. across the load when one diode in a bridge rectifier fails and becomes an open circuit.
items.answer: Only one of the two current paths works, so the output becomes half-wave: one pulse per cycle, ripple frequency halves.
items.markingKey: correct description of output [1]; explanation [1]; quantitative comment (frequency or ripple size) [1] [3]

items.stem: The output of a half-wave rectifier connected to a 50 Hz supply has a peak value of 12 V. A 470 μF smoothing capacitor is connected across a 10 kΩ load. Calculate the time constant of the load and capacitor.

items.stem: The peak power in a resistor connected to a sinusoidal supply is P₀. The mean power is …
items.answer: P₀/2
items.markingKey: Mean of sin² is ½.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Show that the mean power in a resistor carrying a sinusoidal current is half the peak power. (b) Derive the relationship I_rms = I₀/√2 from the definition of r.m.s. value.
items.answer: (a) P = I²R = I₀²R sin²ωt; the mean value of sin²ωt over a cycle is ½, so mean P = ½I₀²R = ½P₀. (b) Mean of I² = I₀² × mean(sin²ωt) = I₀²/2; the square root of this mean is I₀/√2.
items.markingKey: (a) P ∝ sin² [1]; mean of sin² = ½ [1] [2] (b) mean of I² = I₀²/2 [1]; square root [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Derive the relationship I_rms = I₀/√2 from the definition of r.m.s. value. (b) Explain why a lamp connected to a 50 Hz supply does not appear to flicker even though its power varies.
items.answer: (a) Mean of I² = I₀² × mean(sin²ωt) = I₀²/2; the square root of this mean is I₀/√2. (b) The power varies at 100 Hz (twice per cycle) and the filament stays hot between peaks; the eye cannot detect such rapid changes.
items.markingKey: (a) mean of I² = I₀²/2 [1]; square root [1] [2] (b) power peaks at 100 Hz [1]; filament thermal inertia / eye persistence [1] [2]

items.answer: (a) four (b) the conversion of alternating current into direct current

items.stem: Describe and explain the effect on the output p.d. across the load when the load resistance is halved in a smoothed rectifier circuit.
items.answer: RC halves, so the capacitor discharges faster between peaks and the ripple increases (roughly doubles).
items.markingKey: correct description of output [1]; explanation [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Describe how the four diodes in a bridge rectifier ensure the current through the load is always in the same direction. (b) Explain why full-wave rectification gives a smoother output than half-wave rectification for the same smoothing capacitor and load.
items.answer: (a) In each half-cycle a different pair of opposite diodes conducts, both routing the current through the load in the same direction; the other pair is reverse-biased. (b) The capacitor is recharged twice as often (every half-cycle), so it discharges for a shorter time between peaks and the ripple is smaller.
items.markingKey: (a) two diodes conduct each half-cycle [1]; same direction through load both halves [1] [2] (b) twice as many pulses [1]; less time to discharge, smaller ripple [1] [2]

items.answer: (a) In each half-cycle a different pair of opposite diodes conducts, both routing the current through the load in the same direction; the other pair is reverse-biased. (b) The time constant RC increases, so the capacitor discharges more slowly between peaks and the ripple voltage decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) two diodes conduct each half-cycle [1]; same direction through load both halves [1] [2] (b) RC larger [1]; slower discharge, smaller ripple [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how a single capacitor smooths the output of a rectifier. (b) Describe how the four diodes in a bridge rectifier ensure the current through the load is always in the same direction.
items.answer: (a) When the rectified p.d. rises the capacitor charges to the peak; as the p.d. falls the diode stops conducting and the capacitor discharges through the load, keeping the p.d. near the peak until the next pulse recharges it. (b) In each half-cycle a different pair of opposite diodes conducts, both routing the current through the load in the same direction; the other pair is reverse-biased.
items.markingKey: (a) charges at peak [1]; discharges slowly through load between peaks [1] [2] (b) two diodes conduct each half-cycle [1]; same direction through load both halves [1] [2]
